text: Under GDPR Art. 12(3) the controller must act on a rights request within one month of receipt; it can extend by two further months for complex or numerous requests, but must tell the person, with reasons, within the first month.
why: Gives the exact deadline the lecture approximates.

text: The right to erasure is not absolute: GDPR Art. 17(3) lets an organization keep data needed for freedom of expression, legal obligations, public health, archiving or research, or establishing, exercising or defending legal claims.
why: Explains the legitimate way to keep data in cases like harassment.

text: The UK ICO says erasure must also cover backups, but backup data that cannot be overwritten at once can be put 'beyond use': not restored or used for any other purpose, and overwritten on the normal schedule. The individual must be told what happens to their data in backups.
why: States the compliant version of the snapshot practice.

text: GDPR's territorial scope (Art. 3): it applies to organizations established in the EU, and to non-EU organizations that offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour there.

Atlassian's April 2022 outage was caused by a deletion script given site IDs instead of app IDs; it deleted 883 sites for 775 customers, which were restored from 30-day backups over up to 14 days (all by 18 April 2022).
why: Gives the actual cause and the backup recovery behind the anecdote.

text: Client libraries usually do cache compression. pymemcache's CompressedSerde, for example, zlib-compresses values longer than 400 bytes and keeps the original bytes if compression does not make them smaller.
why: Answers the teacher's open 'not sure of any' and shows the size threshold.

text: Redis compresses internally in only two places: strings in RDB snapshot files are LZF-compressed by default (rdbcompression yes), and inner list nodes can be compressed with list-compress-depth (off by default). Ordinary string values in memory are stored as sent.
why: Shows exactly where a cache server compresses on its own.

text: HTTP compression (Gzip, Brotli, Zstandard) helps text such as HTML, CSS, JS and JSON. MDN advises against compressing images, audio and video again, because those formats are already compressed and the overhead can make files larger.
why: Clarifies what CDN-side compression actually helps.

text: Databases read storage in fixed-size pages, 8 kB in PostgreSQL and 16 KB by default in InnoDB, so a 15-byte read and a 1 KB read cost the same single page IO.
InnoDB's buffer pool is an area of main memory that caches table and index data as it is accessed, so frequently used rows are served from RAM, not disk.
why: Shows a database is itself RAM-cached, which narrows the Redis-vs-table gap.

text: A PostgreSQL materialized view stores a query's results in table form. Reads can be far faster than recomputing (the docs show 188 ms dropping to 0.117 ms), but the data is only as fresh as the last REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.
why: A built-in way to do the 'pre-computed table' cache the student proposed.

text: HTTP/1.1 defaults to persistent connections (RFC 9112 9.3); HTTP/1.0 opened a separate TCP connection per request/response unless Keep-Alive was negotiated.
why: Gives the version that each behaviour belongs to.

text: Keep-Alive and Connection are connection-specific headers that HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 forbid; Safari refuses responses that contain them, so the header matters only for HTTP/1.x.
why: Stops readers from adding Keep-Alive headers to HTTP/2 services.

text: WebSocket is a separate TCP-based protocol, but its opening handshake is an HTTP Upgrade request (RFC 6455 1.7), so a WebSocket connection starts as HTTP.
HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC, and QUIC packets are carried in UDP datagrams (RFC 9000), so modern HTTP does run over UDP, with QUIC providing reliability.
why: Resolves the TCP-vs-UDP question with the current standard.

text: As of October 2026, Redis Open Source documents Bloom filters, cuckoo filters, count-min sketch, t-digest, top-k and HyperLogLog as built-in probabilistic data types, along with geospatial indexes, JSON, time series and vector sets.
why: Updates the data-structure list to what current Redis ships.

text: AWS ElastiCache bills serverless caches per GB-hour of data stored plus ElastiCache Processing Units (about 1 ECPU per KB for simple reads and writes), and node-based clusters per node-hour (checked October 2026).
